newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Retail sales seen setting tone.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Retail sales seen setting tone.

text.p: Investors get their first taste of market-moving data this week in the form of retail sales Thursday and economists expected a strong reading on consumer spending in February.

On average, analysts polled by Reuters predicted retail sales would rise 0.6 percent and by 0.7 percent excluding automobile sales. As consumer spending accounts for two-thirds of gross domestic product, policy-makers at the Federal Reserve were certain to pay close attention to the report, due to be released at 830 EST/1330 GMT.

Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities International Inc., forecast sales would rise 0.3 percent overall and by 0.7 percent excluding automobile sales. Auto sales weren't doing all that badly, he added, but would have a tough time maintaining the very high pace seen in January.

"The thing with retail sales is you have to be aware of the unexpected. We don't measure sales all that well and a lot of the time the action's in the revisions," Brusca said. "This is a fairly volatile and highly revised number."
The problem, Brusca said, was analysts had no clue what the revision will look like until they see the number.

Brusca said department store sales were doing well in the month, but cautioned that they only accounted for about 8.0 percent of total retail sales. However, after a strong performance in January he expected continued strong consumer spending in the quarter to date.

"Clearly sentiment is jittery. The market is trading quite sloppily according to our traders," said John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co. He pointed to the market's rebound after the words "moderate" and "temperate" were used in describing wage gains and price pressures in the Fed's Beige Book report on Wednesday.
"Is the Fed going to move or not? Every action is closely scrutinized," Ryding said, ahead of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25.
A Reuters poll of 44 Wall Street economists on Monday showed 17 forecast a rate hike in March, with 34 predicting a tightening by the Fed's subsequent meeting, May 20.
Ryding acknowldged the retail sales number's volatility and sometimes strong revisions. He saw sales up 0.5 percent and rising by 0.7 percent excluding autos.
"We'll react to what the first print says," Ryding said.

Analysts at MMS International said the potential surprise factor for this release lied on the upside. Noting an impressive 0.7 percent increase in personal consumption in January they said there was little reason to expect buying dropped off in April.
"This is a critical time for sales figures -- a few more big ones would change the consumption outlook from one of moderation to one of troublesome acceleration," MMS said.
On Wednesday the Atlanta Fed postponed the release of its manufacturing survey to Thursday at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Jobless claims were set for 830 EST/1330 GMT.
Late Wednesday afternoon three-month bill rates were up two basis points to 5.06 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.18 percent. Year bill rates were also unchanged at 5.38 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 6.10 percent. Five-year notes were down 1/32 at 99-08/32, yielding 6.43 percent. Ten-year notes were down 3/32 to 97-16/32, yielding 6.60 percent.
The 30-year bond was trading off 07/32 at 96-28/32 to yield 6.87 percent.
